subskill: Perpendicular lines: closest point on a line
prompt: In the xy-plane, line l has equation 2x + y = -10, and point P has coordinates (5, 10). Point Q lies on line l, and no other point on line l is closer to P than Q is. What is the x-coordinate of Q?
explanation: The point on a line that is closest to a given point is where the perpendicular from that point meets the line. Line l is y = -2x - 10, so its slope is -2. A line perpendicular to l has slope 1/2 (the negative reciprocal of -2). The perpendicular through P(5, 10) is y - 10 = (1/2)(x - 5), or y = (1/2)x + 7.5. Point Q is where this line meets l: -2x - 10 = (1/2)x + 7.5, so -2.5x = 17.5 and x = -7. Check: Q = (-7, 4), and the segment from Q to P rises 6 while running 12, a slope of 1/2, which is perpendicular to l. The x-coordinate of Q is -7.
solve: const m=-2,c=-10,px=5,py=10; const s=-1/m; const x=(py-s*px-c)/(m-s); return Math.round(x*1e9)/1e9;

distractor_solve.-2.5: const m=-2,c=-10,px=5,py=10; const s=-m; const x=(py-s*px-c)/(m-s); return Math.round(x*1e9)/1e9;
distractor_solve.-15: const m=-2,c=-10,px=5,py=10; const s=1/m; const x=(py-s*px-c)/(m-s); return Math.round(x*1e9)/1e9;

mechanism: closest point = foot of the perpendicular
negative-reciprocal slope through P
intersect with the given line
quantity_asked: x-coordinate of the point Q on line l closest to P

plugback.verify: const y=-10-2*v; const dx=5-v, dy=10-y; return Math.abs(dx*1 + dy*(-2)) < 1e-9;
plugback.why: A student can take an option as the x-coordinate, find the matching y on l, and test whether the segment to P has slope 1/2 (perpendicular to l). That is a check of a few steps per option; in ascending order -15, -10 fail and the key -7 is reached on try 3.

-2.5.why: Negates the slope without taking the reciprocal (uses slope 2 for the perpendicular); nothing in the stem says whether that moves the intersection left or right.

-15.why: Takes the reciprocal but keeps the sign (uses slope -1/2); the side the intersection moves to depends on the geometry, not on any stem wording.

-10.why: Moves P horizontally to l (keeps y = 10) instead of along the perpendicular; whether that point is left or right of the foot is not readable without solving.

counter_error.why: Moving P vertically onto l (keeping x = 5) gives x = 5, above the key; not an option.

shape_check: The stem hands over only a line and a point; Q can be anywhere on l, so any real x is legal. Sign: all four options negative, none excluded. No integer requirement (-2.5 legal). All four survive.
interior_parity_check: Middle values -10 and -7: both negative integers of two characters; the key -7 is not the cleaner one (-10 is rounder).
arith_class_check: Integers: -15, -10, -7 (three of four); odd: -15 and -7; multiples of 5: -15, -10 (and -2.5 is a half-multiple). The key is not alone in any class the stem implies (the stem implies none).

Prior B items SM26F/SM27F use slopes and intercepts but none uses the closest point / perpendicular foot.

A test-wise student might pick the horizontal projection -10 or estimate from a sketch; the sketch shows Q left of P but all four options are left of P. Hard: the decision is recognising that 'closest point' means the perpendicular foot; Desmos needs the student to construct that perpendicular first.

subskill: Linear function from two identities in x
prompt:
A linear function f satisfies both of these identities, each holding for every real number x:
f(x) + f(4 - x) = 6
f(4x) = 4f(x) + 6
Evaluate f(-5).
explanation: Write f(x) = mx + b. Then f(x) + f(4 - x) = mx + b + m(4 - x) + b = 4m + 2b, so 4m + 2b = 6 for every x; equivalently f(2) = 2m + b = 3. Also f(4x) = 4mx + b and 4f(x) + 6 = 4mx + 4b + 6, so b = 4b + 6, which gives -3b = 6 and b = -2. Then 2m - 2 = 3, so m = 2.5, and f(x) = 2.5x - 2. Therefore f(-5) = 2.5(-5) - 2 = -12.5 - 2 = -14.5.
solve: const b=-6/(4-1); const m=(6/2-b)/2; return m*(-5)+b;

distractor_solve.-12.75: const b=-6/4; const m=(6/2-b)/2; return m*(-5)+b;
distractor_solve.-8.25: const b=-6/(4-1); const m=(6/2-b)/4; return m*(-5)+b;
distractor_solve.-0.5: const b=6/(4-1); const m=(6/2-b)/2; return m*(-5)+b;

mechanism: sum identity fixes the value at the midpoint x = 2
scaling identity fixes the intercept
evaluate the line at x = -5
quantity_asked: f(-5) for the linear f determined by two identities

plugback.why: An option gives only one point (-5, v) of the line. To test it a student must still expand the scaling identity to get b = -2 and expand the sum identity to get f(2) = 3, which is the whole solution; once those are known f(-5) follows forward. Checking an option is not cheaper than solving, and neither identity can be tested by substituting a single number.

-12.75.why: Solves b = 4b + 6 as b = -6/4 (divides by 4 instead of 3); the size of that slip on f(-5) depends on the slope that follows, not on stem wording.

-8.25.why: Takes the sum identity to fix f(4) = 3 (the printed 4) instead of f(2) = 3; whether f(-5) rises or falls from that depends on the sign of the evaluation point.

-0.5.why: Solves b = 4b + 6 as b = 2 (sign lost); the effect on f(-5) runs through the recomputed slope and is not readable from the stem.

counter_error.solve: const b=-2; const m=(6-b)/2; return m*(-5)+b;
counter_error.why: Reads the sum identity as f(2) = 6 (forgets that it is twice f(2)); slope 4 gives f(-5) = -22, below the key. Not an option.

cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: none is printed - the stem gives no point value, so f(-5) has no stem-readable bound. Even knowing b = -2 only says f(-5) = -5m - 2, and the sign of m is not visible until f(2) = 3 is found; the distractor -12.75 sits within 2 of the key on its side, so no bound that admits the key strikes all three.
shape_check: The stem hands over only linearity and two identities; f(-5) can be any real (no sign, integrality or cap). All four options legal and survive; the quarter and half values are legal (the slope need not be an integer).
interior_parity_check: Middle values -12.75 and -8.25 (both distractors); the key is extreme.
arith_class_check: Halves: -14.5 and -0.5; quarters: -12.75 and -8.25; no integers; all negative. The key shares its display class (one decimal place, .5) with -0.5, so it is in no singleton class.

subskill: Intercepts of a standard-form line with a constant
prompt: In the xy-plane, the graph of 5x + 11y = k, where k is a constant, is a line. The x-coordinate of its x-intercept is 12 greater than the y-coordinate of its y-intercept. What is the value of k?
explanation: The x-intercept is found by setting y = 0: 5x = k, so x = k/5. The y-intercept is found by setting x = 0: 11y = k, so y = k/11. The condition says k/5 - k/11 = 12. With a common denominator of 55, (11k - 5k)/55 = 12, so 6k/55 = 12 and 6k = 660, giving k = 110. Check: the intercepts are 110/5 = 22 and 110/11 = 10, and 22 - 10 = 12.
mechanism: intercepts of ax + by = k as k/a and k/b
difference of intercepts set equal to 12
solve the linear equation in k

plugback.why: A student can divide an option by 5 and by 11 and test whether the difference is 12. In ascending order 41.25, 60 and 72 fail first, so the key is reached on try 4.

60.why: Sets the x-intercept itself equal to 12 (k/5 = 12) instead of the difference; the y-intercept analogue k/11 = 12 lands above the key, so the stem does not fix a side for this kind of slip.

72.why: Combines k/5 - k/11 as k/(11 - 5) = k/6 (subtracts the denominators); the stem gives no hint of whether that over- or under-states k.

41.25.why: Adds the intercepts instead of subtracting (k/5 + k/11 = 12); nothing in the stem says which side a sum error falls.

counter_error.why: Sets the y-intercept equal to 12 (k/11 = 12), giving k = 132, above the key. Not an option.

cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: with k > 0 the y-intercept is positive, so the x-intercept k/5 is more than 12 and k > 60 - this strikes 41.25 and 60 but not 72, which sits on the key's side of the bound; no single bound strikes all three. The natural errors fall on both sides (k/11 = 12 gives 132 above).
shape_check: Stem properties: 'x-intercept 12 greater than the y-intercept' with coefficients 5 and 11 forces k > 0 (all four options positive, all survive). No integrality is implied (intercepts may be fractions; 41.25 legal). The derived bound k > 60 leaves 72 and 110 together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 60 and 72 are both distractors (the key is extreme); same two-digit integer form.
arith_class_check: Even: 60, 72, 110 (41.25 not an integer). Multiples of 5: 60, 110. Multiples of 11: only 110, but the stem does not imply integer intercepts, so divisibility by 11 is not a class the stem implies; a student testing it is doing the substitution check, which reaches the key on try 4.

subskill: Horizontal gap between two parallel lines
prompt: In the xy-plane, line l has equation 5x - 2y = -18 and line m has equation 15x - 6y = 84. A horizontal line intersects line l at point P and line m at point Q. What is the length of segment PQ?
explanation: Dividing the equation of line m by 3 gives 5x - 2y = 28, so lines l and m are parallel (both have slope 5/2) and a horizontal line meets each of them once. On the horizontal line y = k, point P satisfies 5x - 2k = -18, so x = (2k - 18)/5, and point Q satisfies 5x - 2k = 28, so x = (2k + 28)/5. Since P and Q have the same y-coordinate, PQ is the difference of the x-coordinates: (2k + 28)/5 - (2k - 18)/5 = 46/5 = 9.2. This does not depend on k; for example, on the x-axis P = (-3.6, 0) and Q = (5.6, 0), which are 9.2 units apart.
solve: const c1=-18, c2=84/3, a=5; return Math.round(Math.abs(c2-c1)/a*1e9)/1e9;

distractor_solve.2: const c1=-18, c2=84/3, a=5; return Math.round(Math.abs(c1+c2)/a*1e9)/1e9;

subskill: Linear relation from two readings; where outputs equal inputs
prompt: Two thermometers, A and B, use different temperature scales, and the reading on thermometer B is a linear function of the reading on thermometer A. When thermometer A reads 4 degrees, thermometer B reads 31 degrees, and when thermometer A reads 19 degrees, thermometer B reads 37 degrees. At what reading of thermometer A will the two thermometers show the same reading?
explanation: Let a be the reading on thermometer A and b the reading on thermometer B. The rate of change of b with respect to a is (37 - 31)/(19 - 4) = 6/15 = 0.4. Using the point (4, 31), b - 31 = 0.4(a - 4), so b = 0.4a + 29.4. The two readings are the same when b = a: a = 0.4a + 29.4, so 0.6a = 29.4 and a = 49. Check: when thermometer A reads 49, thermometer B reads 0.4(49) + 29.4 = 19.6 + 29.4 = 49.
solve: const a1=4,b1=31,a2=19,b2=37; const m=(b2-b1)/(a2-a1); const c=b1-m*a1; return Math.round(c/(1-m)*1e9)/1e9;

distractor_solve.21: const a1=4,b1=31,a2=19,b2=37; const m=(b2-b1)/(a2-a1); const c=b1-m*a1; return Math.round(c/(1+m)*1e9)/1e9;
distractor_solve.39: const a1=4,b1=31,a2=19,b2=37; const m=(b2-b1)/(a2-a1); const c=b1-m*a2; return Math.round(c/(1-m)*1e9)/1e9;

mechanism: rate of change from two paired readings
intercept of the linear relation
solve b = a for the reading both scales share
quantity_asked: the thermometer-A reading at which both thermometers show the same number

-73.5.why: Sets thermometer B's reading to 0 instead of setting the two readings equal (solves 0 = 0.4a + 29.4); nothing in the stem says which side of the shared reading that lands.

No single bound strikes all three, and the intercept sign slip (54.33...) falls above the key.

subskill: Line from a point and a stated rate; sum of its intercepts
prompt: In the xy-plane, line l passes through the point (3, -10). Along line l, for every increase of 6 in x, y decreases by 3. What is the sum of the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of line l and the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of line l?
explanation: The slope of line l is -3/6 = -1/2. Using the point (3, -10), y - (-10) = -(1/2)(x - 3), so y = -(1/2)x + 1.5 - 10 = -(1/2)x - 8.5. The y-coordinate of the y-intercept is -8.5. For the x-intercept, set y = 0: 0 = -(1/2)x - 8.5, so x = -17. The sum is -17 + (-8.5) = -25.5.
solve: const p=3,q=-10,m=-3/6; const b=q-m*p; return b+(-b/m);

distractor_solve.-6: const p=3,q=-10,m=-6/3; const b=q-m*p; return b+(-b/m);
distractor_solve.11.5: const p=3,q=-10,m=3/6; const b=q-m*p; return b+(-b/m);

mechanism: slope from a stated rate of change
point-slope form to the y-intercept
x-intercept from the equation, then add the two intercepts
quantity_asked: x-coordinate of the x-intercept plus y-coordinate of the y-intercept of line l

plugback.why: The ask is a sum of two intercepts, not a value that satisfies any printed equation or condition. An option cannot be substituted anywhere in the stem; testing it requires building the line and finding both intercepts, which is the whole solution.

-6.why: Takes the slope as -6/3 = -2 (change in x over change in y); both intercepts move, in amounts that depend on the point, so the stem does not show which way the sum goes.

11.5.why: Uses slope +1/2, ignoring 'decreases'; the y-intercept falls while the x-intercept jumps to the other side, so the net effect on the sum is not readable from the stem.

-17.why: Finds the x-intercept and stops without adding the y-intercept; whether the omitted -8.5 is positive or negative is only known after solving.

counter_error.solve: const p=3,q=-10,m=-3/6; const b=q+m*p; return b+(-b/m);
counter_error.why: Writes y = -(1/2)x + (-10 - 1.5) (sign slip expanding the point-slope form), so the y-intercept is -11.5 and the x-intercept -23: sum -34.5, below the key. Not an option.

cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: a line with negative slope through (3, -10) has a y-intercept above -10 but the stem does not tell its sign without computing -10 + 1.5; even granting both intercepts negative only strikes 11.5, and -17 and -6 sit on the key's side of it. The point-slope sign slip (-34.5) lands below the key, so the errors split.
shape_check: The stem hands over a line with a stated rate and one point; the sum of the intercepts can be any real number (no sign, integer or cap implied). All four options are legal; -25.5, -17 and -6 together survive 'sum negative', and every option survives 'not necessarily an integer'.
interior_parity_check: Middle values -17 and -6 are both negative integers (both distractors; the key is extreme).
arith_class_check: Halves: -25.5 and 11.5; integers: -17 and -6. Negative: -25.5, -17, -6. The key shares its display class (.5) with 11.5 and its sign with two distractors, so it is alone in no class.

subskill: Linear model from two readings; input that doubles the intercept
prompt: The length of a spring is a linear function of the mass hanging from it. When a 60-gram mass hangs from the spring, the spring is 14.4 centimeters long, and when a 110-gram mass hangs from it, the spring is 17.6 centimeters long. According to this model, what mass, in grams, would make the spring twice as long as it is with no mass hanging from it?
explanation: The length increases by 17.6 - 14.4 = 3.2 centimeters when the mass increases by 110 - 60 = 50 grams, so the rate of change is 3.2/50 = 0.064 centimeter per gram. With no mass, the length is 14.4 - 0.064(60) = 14.4 - 3.84 = 10.56 centimeters, so the model is L = 10.56 + 0.064m. Twice the length with no mass is 2(10.56) = 21.12 centimeters: 10.56 + 0.064m = 21.12, so 0.064m = 10.56 and m = 165 grams.
solve: const m1=60,L1=14.4,m2=110,L2=17.6; const s=(L2-L1)/(m2-m1); const n=L1-s*m1; return Math.round(n/s*1e9)/1e9;

distractor_solve.88: const m1=60,L1=14.4,m2=110,L2=17.6; const s=(L2-L1)/(m2-m1); const n=L1-s*m1; return Math.round(2*n/(L1/m1)*1e9)/1e9;
distractor_solve.115: const m1=60,L1=14.4,m2=110,L2=17.6; const s=(L2-L1)/(m2-m1); const n=L1-s*m2; return Math.round(n/s*1e9)/1e9;
distractor_solve.132: const m1=60,L1=14.4,m2=110,L2=17.6; const s=(L2-L1)/(m2-m1); const n=L1-s*m1; return Math.round(2*n/(L2/m2)*1e9)/1e9;

mechanism: rate of change from two paired readings
intercept = length with no mass
solve for the mass giving twice the intercept
quantity_asked: mass that makes the spring twice its no-mass length

plugback.verify: const s=(17.6-14.4)/(110-60); const n=14.4-s*60; return Math.abs(n+s*v-2*n) < 1e-9;
plugback.why: After building L = 10.56 + 0.064m, a student can compute the length for an option and compare it with 2(10.56). The model itself (rate and intercept) must be derived first, and in ascending order 88, 115 and 132 fail before the key, which is reached on try 4.

88.why: Finds the no-mass length but then uses length per gram of the 60-gram reading (14.4/60) as the rate instead of the rate of change; the stem does not show whether that ratio is larger or smaller than the true rate.

115.why: Computes the no-mass length with a mismatched pair (14.4 with the 110-gram mass); whether the crossed pair raises or lowers the intercept depends on which readings are crossed, not on stem wording.

132.why: Same proportional slip using the 110-gram reading (17.6/110); a different reading gives a different ratio, and neither its size nor its side is visible from the stem.

counter_error.solve: const m1=60,L1=14.4,m2=110,L2=17.6; const s=(L2-L1)/(m2-m1); const n=L1+s*m1; return n/s;
counter_error.why: Adds instead of subtracts when finding the no-mass length (14.4 + 3.84 = 18.24), then solves correctly: 285 grams, above the key. Not an option.

cheap_bound_check: Cheapest one-sided bound: the spring stretches, so doubling the no-mass length needs a mass beyond 110 grams only if 17.6 is less than twice the unknown no-mass length - not readable without computing it. Granting 'more than 110 grams' strikes 88 only; 115 and 132 sit on the key's side. The intercept sign slip (285) lands above the key, so the errors split.
shape_check: A mass is positive: all four options positive. No integer requirement (the readings are decimals). All four survive; 115, 132 and 165 together survive 'more than 110 grams'.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 115 and 132 are both three-digit integers (both distractors; the key is extreme).
arith_class_check: All integers. Odd: 115 and 165; multiples of 11: 88, 132, 165; multiples of 5: 115 and 165. The key shares every class with at least one distractor.
